background.definition: Scrotal swelling may be due to extratesticular and intratesticular lesions. Most extratesticular lesions are benign, while the majority of intratesticular lesions are malignant.

list.listitem: Most hydroceles are congenital and noted in infancy but may affect affect 1% of adult males.
Varicoceles occur in up to 15% to 20% of adolescents and young adults.
Testicular cancers make up 1% of all male malignancies between ages 20 and 35 years; they are more common in white than in African Americans.
Testicular lymphoma accounts for 1% to 7% of all testicular neoplasms; lymphoma is the most common malignant testicular tumor in men over 50 years.
The incidence of hernia increases with age, from 1% in men younger than 45 years old to 3% to 5% in those older than 45 years.
Testicular cancer: approximately 5500 new cases per year in the United States.
Testicular tumors: 4/100,000 in males between 20 to 35 years of age.
See Differential Diagnosis section below.
Four common causes: spermatocele, hydrocele, varicocele, and tumor
The most common testicular tumor is seminoma

In a series of 230 adults presenting with acute or subacute scrotal pain or painless enlargement of the scrotum, final diagnoses were as follows: epididymo-orchitis (80), torsion (29), trauma (23), neoplasm (18), hydrocele (13), varicocele (10), tumor-like conditions (6), Fournier gangrene (3), and inguinial hernia (3).
Testicular adrenal rest tumors are intratesticular masses that occur in male patients with CAH

Differential.Differential_Features: Soft mass (bag of worms), left-sided usually; palpate in standing position (Valsalva maneuver)
Intermittent swelling, Risk of incarceration (lack of peristalsis)
Usually painless, does not transilluminate, firm or hard

Differential.Differential_Name: Rare: neuroblastoma, lymphoma, Hemoch Schoenlein Purpura (HSP), sarcoidosis, coccidiodomycosis, leukemic infiltration, rhabdomyosarcoma, Leydig cell tumor, and neuroectodermal tumor
Intra-abdominal process such as ruptured appendicitis
Differential.Differential_Features: Sick looking, painful, abdominal pain and tenderness

list.listitem: Painless causes: hydrocele, varicocele, and spermatocele
Painful causes: testicular torsion, epididymitis and orchitis

Hernia: typically presents as a nontender swelling that is reducible and enlarges with standing or with increases in intra-abdominal pressure. Indirect inguinal hernias usually present during the first year of life while direct hernia occur in older patients.
Varicocele: usually a "bag of worms" consistency, which is prominent when the patient stands. Valsalva maneuver can increase the degree of dilation, usually left sided.
Spermatocele: frequently involves the upper pole or epididymal head; transilluminating cystic mass located above and separate from the testis.
Hydrocele: nontender, cystic, transilluminating mass that lies anterior to the testis.
Testicular malignancy: typically a hard or firm, nontender intratesticular mass.

For patients with a painful scrotal mass when torsion is possible, emergent referral to a urologist is preferred over delay to order imaging studies. Ultrasound is 88% sensitive and 90% specific for detecting torsion. Radionuclide imaging is also accurate, but takes even longer than ultrasound at most institutions.

Ultrasound with Doppler flow study is the initial study of choice in all patients with a painless scrotal mass. Ultrasound is 90% to 100% accurate in differentiating intratesticular from paratesticular mass and can usually differentiate masses such as hydrocele, inguinal hernia, and varicocele. Hydroceles transilluminate, whereas solid scrotal masses do not. When used with color flow Doppler, it is almost 100% sensitive and specific in detecting varicocele. A prospective study of 236 patients (age range 0-53 years) with clinically suspected torsion found 100% sensitivity using color coded duplex sonography, with 100% negative predictive value. Ultrasound is also nearly 100% sensitive for the detection of testicular neoplasms with a negative-predictive value of almost 100%.

A hypoechogenic mass within the testis is presumed to be testicular cancer and requires referral to a urologist. MRI may be helpful to differentiate between benign and malignant lesions. If a testicular tumor is supected, perform CT of the abdomen and pelvis (to detect metastasis to the retroperitoneal lymph nodes) and chest CT (to detect mediastinal, hilar, or lung parenchymal disease). Obtain tumor markers (serum human chorionic gonadotrophin, alpha-fetoprotein, and lactate dehydrogenase) at the initial presentation if testicular tumor is suspected, as they are elevated in up to 70% of patients with testicular cancer.
Inguinal hernia: diagnosis of hernia is primarily clinical. However, in equivocal cases, ultrasound can be helpful in making the diagnosis.
Testicular torsion; testis is enlarged, less dense, and less echogenic. Color Doppler shows decreased blood flow.

Acute idiopathic scrotal edema is a diagnosis of exclusion; ultrasound may show "fountain sign" increased blood flow in the peritesticular scrotal soft tissue resembling colored fountain (due to intense hyperemia).

A clinical decision rule called the Testicular Workup for Ischemia and Suspected Torsion (TWIST) score assigned 2 points for testicular swelling, 2 points for hard testicle, and 1 point each for absent cremasteric reflex, nausea or vomiting, and high riding testis. It is an effective tool for suspected testicular torsion. In their initial validation study they found 100% negative predictive value for a score less than or equal to 2 points, and 100% positive predictive value for a score of 5 points or higher.
A key determination is whether the mass is intra- or extratesticular. Consider intratesticular masses malignant until malignancy is ruled out.
If pain is present, especially if acute, always consider testicular torsion in the differential diagnosis and urgently refer to a urologist if suspected.
